content: The detection of circulating virus by nucleic acid testing (NAT) is inherently associated with active infection, and the reference standard used in these studies is highly specific. In the domain of flow and timing (PICO 5a), 42 studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias, while eight studies were deemed to have an unclear risk of bias. In seven studies, it was not possible to determine whether the index and reference tests were performed on the same specimen or within one month. In one study, the number of participants was unknown, making it impossible to confirm if all were included in the final analysis. For PICO 9, four studies were judged to have a low risk of bias because the index and reference tests were performed on the same specimens at various time points, and all patients were included in the final analyses. However, one study was considered high risk because not all enrolled patients were included in the analysis, only those who completed the protocol. Regarding the use of HCV core antigen (HCVcAg) for diagnosing active HCV infection, the Abbott ARCHITECT assay was evaluated in 20 studies with a total of 11,820 samples. An additional 10 studies contributed data for sensitivity analysis, involving 12,788 samples. The pooled sensitivity and specificity estimates were calculated for all samples, HCV antibody-positive samples, and HCV antibody-negative samples. The summary points in the plots for antibody-positive and all samples approached the upper left corner, indicating good diagnostic accuracy of the ARCHITECT test. However, the plot for antibody-negative specimens showed a broad 95% confidence interval, reflecting variability. Heterogeneity was visually assessed and found to be relatively low, but meta-regression was not feasible due to limited data on predefined covariates. Three outlier studies (Ergünay, Florea, and Gu) reported sensitivities of 72%, 74%, and 44%, respectively. Specificity results were more homogeneous, with only one outlier (the Medici study), which lacked demographic data as it was conducted on anonymous samples. Genotype distribution was reported in 15 studies, with genotype 1b being the most prevalent, while genotypes 5 and 6 were minimally studied. The Ortho ELISA-Ag test was evaluated in five studies with 1,177 total samples. The pooled sensitivity and specificity estimates suggested good diagnostic accuracy, but the data exhibited some heterogeneity, as demonstrated by the wide 95% confidence intervals. Two outlier studies (Nübling and El-Sayed) reported unknown HIV or HBV coinfection status, and genotype distribution was unknown for El-Sayed. The studies were conducted on plasma samples collected at various time points during HCV infection, with varying levels of HCV RNA. The data were not stratified by antibody status, and raw quantitative information was unavailable. The Bio-Rad Monolisa HCV Ag-Ab ULTRA test was assessed in five studies with 525 total samples. Due to observed heterogeneity in the forest plot, a pooled analysis was not performed, and only descriptive statistics were examined. All studies were conducted in participants with 100% HIV coinfection, but genotype distribution varied. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 33% for genotype 1a to 0% for genotype 3. Sensitivity improved to 71% when limited to specimens with HCV RNA >10^6 IU/mL, but remained negative in genotype 3 samples with viral loads >2 million IU/mL. The EIKEN Lumispot HCV Ag assay was evaluated in two studies. One study reported 100% sensitivity, suggesting a bias toward better performance, but specificity data were insufficient. The Hunan Jynda Bioengineering Group HCV Core Ag ELISA was assessed in four studies with 524 total samples. Heterogeneity among the studies limited confidence in the pooled estimate, and no covariate assessment was performed due to unknown HIV, HBV, and genotype distribution. The Murex Ag/Ab EIA test was evaluated in four studies with a total sample size of 770. Substantial heterogeneity in the forest plot precluded pooled analysis. Sensitivity estimates ranged from 50% to 100%, with specificity not calculable. The study was conducted in HCV antibody-negative specimens during the acute infection window period. Sensitivity increased from 50% to 98% when limited to specimens with viral loads >10^6 IU/mL. The Fujirebio Lumipulse test was assessed in two studies. The Takahashi study included 60 genotype 1b patients and 30 genotype 2 patients. Serum HCV core antigen was measured at baseline and at multiple time points during treatment. Sustained virologic response (SVR) was achieved in 50% of genotype 1b patients and 90% of genotype 2 patients. In genotype 1b patients, HCVcAg levels were higher in the non-SVR group compared to the SVR group, while no difference was observed in genotype 2 patients. The Fujino study enrolled 49 genotype 1b patients, with 44 completing the protocol. SVR was achieved in 10 patients. HCVcAg and RNA were measured on days 1, 7, and 14 of therapy. Four SVR patients had negative HCVcAg on day 1, while all had positive NAT results. This systematic review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of HCV core antigen tests for identifying active HCV infection and for treatment monitoring. The ARCHITECT assay was the most extensively studied and demonstrated the highest precision in sensitivity and specificity estimates. However, data on genotypes 4, 5, and 6 were largely lacking, and most studies were conducted in high-resource settings, limiting generalizability to lowand middle-income countries. Further research is needed to assess test performance in routine laboratory settings and to evaluate the utility of HCVcAg for treatment monitoring and as a predictor of SVR.
